question: When studying community health, what does 'incidence' mainly measure?

options.A: The total number of existing cases at one time
options.B: The financial cost of managing an outbreak
options.C: The frequency of new cases of a disease
options.D: The percentage of people who die from a condition

explanation: You've got this! Incidence simply means tracking the brand-new cases of a health condition popping up over a specific time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why do public health nurses and planners care about measuring disease incidence?

options.A: It provides the exact medical cure for infected patients
options.B: It shows if a disease outbreak is growing or shrinking
options.C: It replaces the need for routine vaccination programs
options.D: It calculates the total hospital building costs needed

explanation: Spot-on! Watching new cases over time helps health teams know if prevention is working or if an epidemic is spreading. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: When calculating the incidence of a disease, what goes on top (the numerator)?

options.A: The number of new cases developed during a period
options.B: The entire population living in the community
options.C: The number of patients who recovered completely
options.D: The total number of people who died from old age

explanation: Great job! The numerator in an incidence formula always focuses strictly on the newly diagnosed cases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: If you are calculating the incidence of a uterine infection, who belongs at the bottom (the denominator)?

options.A: Every single person living in the entire country
options.B: All children under the age of five years old
options.C: Only individuals with a uterus who are at risk
options.D: Only patients who already have the infection

explanation: Well done! The denominator should only include the people who are actually at risk of catching that specific condition. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: How is prevalence different from incidence?

options.A: Prevalence counts both old and new cases together
options.B: Prevalence is calculated without using a denominator
options.C: Prevalence only measures diseases that last one day
options.D: Prevalence ignores people who are currently receiving care

explanation: Think of prevalence as the big picture: it adds up all existing cases, while incidence only counts the fresh, new ones! [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: A village has had 500 total cases of diabetes for ten years, but only 5 people were newly diagnosed this year. What does this mean?

options.A: Both high prevalence and high incidence
options.B: Both low prevalence and low incidence

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! A large total of ongoing cases means high prevalence, while just a few fresh diagnoses means low incidence. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is another popular name for cumulative incidence?
explanation: Easy peasy! Cumulative incidence is often called incidence proportion because it shows the proportion of the group that gets sick over time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: When would a researcher prefer to use 'incidence density' instead of cumulative incidence?

options.A: When every single person stays in the study until the end
options.B: When calculating the prevalence of a permanent birth defect
options.C: When study participants enter at different times or drop out
options.D: When the researcher only cares about counting total deaths

explanation: Incidence density uses person-time, which is a lifesaver when people join a study at different times or drop out along the way. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: Which of these does NOT normally change the incidence of a disease in a population?

options.A: The introduction of better diagnostic testing tools
options.B: The total number of historical hospital building designs

explanation: Correct! Hospital architecture won't directly stop or spread infections the way vaccines or environmental changes do. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: Why might a clinic suddenly record a higher incidence of a disease after getting a brand-new testing machine?

options.A: The disease has suddenly stopped spreading entirely
options.B: More mild or early cases are successfully detected
options.C: The total population at risk has decreased to zero
options.D: People have completely stopped visiting health clinics

explanation: Better testing tools simply help us catch infections that used to fly under the radar, making the recorded new cases go up! [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is one of the main ways community health nurses use incidence data?

options.A: Managing the stock of non-medical office stationery
options.B: Spotting unusual disease spikes to trigger quick responses
options.C: Determining the structural engineering needs of bridges
options.D: Calculating the personal income tax of local residents

explanation: Exactly! Nurses keep an eye on incidence so they can spot outbreaks early and jump into action to protect the community. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)

question: A community nurse notices a sudden weekly jump in new diarrhea cases in a local village. What should be done first?

options.A: Assume the data collection error is harmless and ignore it
options.B: Wait until the end of the year to calculate annual prevalence
options.C: Close all local schools permanently without further testing
options.D: Investigate possible sources like contaminated water supplies

explanation: Brilliant clinical thinking! A sudden spike means you need to hunt down the source—like bad drinking water—right away to stop the spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)
